general.temas: Crime stories, including killings and sexual offences, appear on several front pages. Political and legal news also recurs, particularly concerning Donald Trump, as do references to Russia and security. The Daily Mirror alone highlights difficulties accessing NHS dentistry.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions stand at 58 out of 100 because of political and legal clashes and the abundance of violent incidents. In the UK, the Daily Mail reports on the clash between Kemi Badenoch and the prime minister, while the Mirror reflects criticism of Nigel Farage over his Brexit campaign. In the United States, a court ruling challenges Trump’s position on citizenship; the war in Ukraine and nuclear fears also feature. Sport, health and leisure provide less contentious news.

The Telegraph.resumen:
- Esther Rantzen, presenter and founder of Childline, dies aged 86.
- The front page highlights several violent incidents, including the death of a girl in Surrey and a stabbing in Northampton.
- Counterterrorism police are investigating a vehicle fire outside a London synagogue, allegedly linked to Iran.
- The government is preparing measures against foreign political donations and the use of shell companies.
- Also featured are forecasts of threats for 2026, criticism of the “woke” left, press award nominations and a play on words.
The Telegraph.motivo_populismo: The score reflects disparaging expressions such as “the woke left has started to devour itself”, alongside an alarmist tone in a warning about a possible pandemic worse than Covid.
The Telegraph.sesgo: The selection devotes considerable space to violent incidents and threats, emphasising a focus on security and risk. An opinion article also takes an explicitly critical stance towards the “woke” left.

The Independent.resumen:
- Manchester United features in several stories about penalties and a disallowed goal against Sporting.
- A storm forces the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to be postponed for the first time.
- ICE detains a migrant who had won the lottery; a judge rejects Trump’s position on birthright citizenship.
- Six family members die in a plane crash and suspected sabotage forces a Christmas display in Nebraska to close.
- Other prominent stories cover memory and blood sugar, Black Friday deals and data centres in space.
The Independent.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “horror show”, “from hero to zero” and “throws the Supreme Court in his face” dramatise events, although there are few discernible appeals to the people against the elites.
The Independent.sesgo: The front page prioritises sport, crime and conflict, with often sensationalist wording. Political coverage is notably critical of Trump’s immigration and citizenship measures.

Daily Mail.resumen:
- A woman is banned from Marks & Spencer for damaging clothes and requesting refunds; studies on sex and pornography also feature prominently.
- Raheem Sterling receives a suspended prison sentence after a crash; a television florist fatally ran over a woman.
- A Reform councillor appears in court accused of sexual offences and making threats; a police chief is convicted of rape and sexual assault.
- Kemi Badenoch criticises the prime minister over a video of guests at Downing Street; another story shows forced recruitment in Ukraine.
- A feature examines data centres; Josef Fritzl’s lawyer wins a legal case over topless photos of herself.
Daily Mail.motivo_populismo: Sensationalist expressions such as “mysterious centres”, “dragged off the street” and “Kemi lashes out” abound, alongside capital letters and direct appeals to the reader, although there is little framing of the people against the elites.
Daily Mail.sesgo: The selection prioritises sexual offences, crime, celebrities and controversies, with an emotional and attention-grabbing approach. Political coverage emphasises verbal confrontation, while technology coverage highlights potential threats before explaining its function.

Daily Mirror.resumen:
- Millions of people cannot access NHS dentists and some resort to pulling out their own teeth.
- A body is found in the search for Kelsey Hunter; other stories cover criminal cases and the deaths of at least 30 people in a fire in Cairo.
- European leaders fear Russia could deploy a nuclear weapon in orbit before the end of the year.
- The front page covers Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC and criticism of Farage’s campaign in support of Brexit.
- Energy bills, pensions information and the latest news from “I’m A Celebrity” also feature prominently.
Daily Mirror.motivo_populismo: Alarmist and sensationalist expressions abound, such as “extreme measures”, “fireball”, “evil” and “he is trapped”, although there is little explicit opposition between the people and the elites.
Daily Mirror.sesgo: The selection emphasises social hardship, particularly in healthcare and energy, and treats crime and disaster stories dramatically. In politics, the wording presents Trump and Farage critically.

opiniones.comunista:
Today I see the class struggle in an unbearable scene: people who cannot find an NHS dentist or afford a private one are driven to pull out their own teeth. Health should not depend on the size of your wallet. I support publicly provided dentistry accessible to all, funded according to each person’s ability to pay.

The same inequality appears in energy: struggling households in homes that leak heat face some of the highest bills. It is not enough to ask them to consume less; we need publicly funded home improvements and collective ownership of energy, under democratic control, so that a basic necessity is not subordinated to profit.

I also welcome the desire to limit the influence of shell companies in political donations. But a democracy worthy of the name must confront the power of big capital in general, not only when the money comes from abroad.
opiniones.anarquista:
The fact that millions of people cannot access an NHS dentist while others face disproportionate energy bills reveals more than an administrative failure: basic needs remain subordinated to money and to decisions made far from those who suffer the consequences. I do not trust another party or regulation of political donations to give us back control. I would rather build it from the ground up: energy cooperatives, mutual aid networks and health services managed by professionals and communities, with resources accessible to all.

The vehicle fire outside a synagogue, being investigated as an antisemitic hate incident, also demands a collective response. Freedom does not exist if a community lives under threat. Solidarity among neighbours, regardless of origin or belief, is a defence against hate and against the temptation to hand even more power to the authorities.
opiniones.liberal:
The crisis in public dentistry concerns me: when people cannot get care and are driven to pull out their own teeth, it is not enough to defend the system as it stands. I would open up more room for competition and patient choice, with targeted assistance for those who need it, rather than trusting an ever-expanding state to solve everything.

I also support clear rules against foreign political donations concealed behind shell companies. Protecting democracy requires transparency, but without treating every legitimate contribution as suspicious or unnecessarily restricting political expression.

And I welcome a judge’s reminder that a president cannot unilaterally change citizenship rules. For me, freedom requires limits on power, low taxes and personal responsibility; not privileges for those in government or indifference to those who suffer.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
Today I see a country that needs to regain control of its decisions and fulfil its most basic duties. I support tightening the rules against foreign political donations: no shell company should be allowed to buy influence in our democracy. But sovereignty also requires defending Brexit and strict immigration controls, decided by the British people rather than by elites who distrust their own electorate.

The investigation into the fires outside a London synagogue is a reminder that security is not a slogan: the state must protect British Jews and pursue any foreign interference, without prejudging the police’s conclusions. And when millions cannot afford a dentist, our leaders should attend to the needs of people here first. A strong nation protects its borders, its traditions and its citizens.
opiniones.centro:
I am concerned that millions of people cannot access an NHS dentist and that some are driven to pull out their own teeth. Dental care should not depend on how much each family can afford to pay. I would favour gradual reform, with stable funding and agreements with professionals to expand public provision. The private sector can complement the service, but it cannot replace the guarantee of access for those with the least.

I also welcome efforts to tighten the rules on foreign political donations and shell companies. Transparency protects democratic competition without prohibiting legitimate participation. This is a reform that should be built through parliamentary consensus and implemented with independent oversight. For me, reliable institutions and accessible public services are not opposing projects: both sustain the trust that a democracy needs.
